chunks: From him, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Aban, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abdillah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

Indeed, Umm Abdillah bint al-Harith wanted to have a Mus'haf (copy of the Quran) written, so she bought paper from her own stock and invited a man to write for her without a specific condition (fixed wage). When he finished, she gave him fifty dinars. And indeed, the Mus'hafs were not sold except as new items.

key_terms.الْمَصَاحِفُ: The plural of Mus'haf, referring to copies of the Quran
key_terms.خَمْسِينَ دِينَارًا: Fifty dinars (a significant sum of gold currency)
key_terms.مُصْحَفًا: A copy of the Quran, specifically one written on paper

ai.seo_question: How is the wage determined for copying the Quran if no specific price is agreed upon beforehand?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the distinction between a fixed-price contract (*ujra*) and a gift (*hibah*) in the context of Quranic transcription, where the absence of a pre-agreed wage allowed the employer to bestow fifty dinars as a generous reward. It further reflects the historical economic reality that early Quranic manuscripts were treated as valuable, pristine commodities, rarely sold as second-hand goods, thereby emphasizing the sanctity and high value placed on the physical text of the Quran in Shia jurisprudence.
